results.name: single_example_generalization_rate
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets on sets with exactly one example; observed above null means people generalize more broadly from a single example than the model's size principle allows (below = more conservative).
results.code:
# name: single_example_generalization_rate
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets on sets with exactly one example; observed above null means people generalize more broadly from a single example than the model's size principle allows (below = more conservative).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    n_ex = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = (n_ex == 1) & ~is_ex
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: same_parity_set_opposite_parity_targets
results.description: Yes rate for targets of the opposite parity to the examples, on sets of 3+ examples that are all odd or all even; observed below null means people respect the examples' shared parity more strictly than the model (above = less strictly).
results.code:
# name: same_parity_set_opposite_parity_targets
# description: Yes rate for targets of the opposite parity to the examples, on sets of 3+ examples that are all odd or all even; observed below null means people respect the examples' shared parity more strictly than the model (above = less strictly).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    n_ex = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, np.mod(ex, 2))
    all_odd = np.nansum(par == 1, axis=1) == n_ex
    all_even = np.nansum(par == 0, axis=1) == n_ex
    tp = t % 2
    m = (n_ex >= 3) & ((all_odd & (tp == 0)) | (all_even & (tp == 1)))
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: above_minus_below_range
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples, yes rate of targets above the examples' max minus yes rate of targets below the examples' min; observed above null means people extrapolate upward more (and downward less) than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: above_minus_below_range
# description: For sets of 2+ examples, yes rate of targets above the examples' max minus yes rate of targets below the examples' min; observed above null means people extrapolate upward more (and downward less) than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    n_ex = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    above = (n_ex >= 2) & (t > hi)
    below = (n_ex >= 2) & (t < lo)
    if above.sum() == 0 or below.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[above].mean() - r[below].mean())

results.name: in_range_shared_decade_effect
results.description: For non-example targets inside the min-max range of sets with 2+ examples, yes rate of targets sharing a tens digit with some example minus those sharing none; observed above null means people use decade (place-value) similarity more than the model's rule/interval hypotheses predict.
results.code:
# name: in_range_shared_decade_effect
# description: For non-example targets inside the min-max range of sets with 2+ examples, yes rate of targets sharing a tens digit with some example minus those sharing none; observed above null means people use decade (place-value) similarity more than the model's rule/interval hypotheses predict.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    n_ex = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    tens_ex = np.floor(ex / 10)
    share = (tens_ex == np.floor(t / 10)[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    ok = (n_ex >= 2) & ~is_ex & (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a, b = ok & share, ok & ~share
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: example_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials whose target is itself one of the shown examples; observed below null means people endorse the examples themselves less than the model (which treats examples as near-certain members) predicts.

results.name: last_minus_first_nearest_example
results.description: For non-example targets on sets of 2+ examples, yes rate when the numerically nearest example is the last-shown one minus when it is the first-shown one; observed above null means a recency effect (the last example pulls generalization more than the order-invariant model predicts), below null a primacy effect.
results.code:
# name: last_minus_first_nearest_example
# description: For non-example targets on sets of 2+ examples, yes rate when the numerically nearest example is the last-shown one minus when it is the first-shown one; observed above null means a recency effect (the last example pulls generalization more than the order-invariant model predicts), below null a primacy effect.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    n_ex = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    d = np.abs(ex - t[:, None])
    d = np.where(np.isnan(d), np.inf, d)
    nearest = np.argmin(d, axis=1)
    dmin = d.min(axis=1)
    ties = (d == dmin[:, None]).sum(axis=1) > 1
    ok = (n_ex >= 2) & ~is_ex & ~ties
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    last = ok & (nearest == n_ex - 1)
    first = ok & (nearest == 0)
    if last.sum() == 0 or first.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[last].mean() - r[first].mean())

results.name: cell_extremity_fraction
results.description: Fraction of (set, target) cells whose mean yes rate is <= 0.15 or >= 0.85; observed above null means human judgments are more all-or-none (the model's predictions are too graded/intermediate), below null means they are more graded than the model.

results.name: trial_index_drift
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and rating across all trials; observed differing from null (near 0, the model has no time dependence) means yes-rate drifts over the session (positive = more yes later, negative = fewer).
